solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Adjusted damages agent effectively arranged (5-7)

indicatorNotes.Adjusted: the letters of the fodder are adjusted into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An insurance claim where the payout was tweaked by an agent who knew how to work the system.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is an insurance or legal story, so 'damages agent' reads as a phrase; it is just twelve letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Something stage-managed has been arranged behind the scenes to come off effectively, like a well-run show.

entries.clue: Dog found briefly in experimental area (8)

annotation.definition: Dog found briefly in experimental area

blocks.note: the surface hears a dog turning up for a moment; the setter means the dog's name found in its brief, shortened form
that short form is also the everyday word for a laboratory

annotation.surface: A dog wanders for a moment into a research laboratory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' looks like an instruction to cut a word, but it describes the dog's name: shortened, a Labrador is a LAB, the same word as the experimental area.
annotation.definitionFit: The Labrador is a breed of dog, commonly called a lab.

entries.clue: Put money on a second-class mark (4)

blocks.note: to bet is to put money on
kept as it is

annotation.surface: A gambler backs a horse that only gets a second-rate rating.
annotation.walkthrough: In British marking, a beta is a second-class grade, below alpha, as in a 'beta plus' essay.
annotation.definitionFit: Beta, the second Greek letter, is used as a grade for second-class work.

entries.clue: Feature of derelict apse and court (6)

indicatorNotes.derelict: a derelict building has fallen apart, so its letters are in ruins

blocks.note: APSE rearranged
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

annotation.surface: A tour of a ruined church points out its crumbling apse and courtyard.
annotation.walkthrough: An apse is the rounded end of a church; here it is only four letters to rearrange before CT is added.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one facet or characteristic of something, which is what a feature is.

entries.clue: Scout’s former partner given new role in public relations (8)

indicatorNotes.new: the letters of ROLE are made new, in a fresh order
indicatorNotes.in: the new letters go inside PR

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
PR = public relations
ROLE rearranged, placed inside PR

annotation.surface: A scout's ex-partner lands a new job in PR.
annotation.walkthrough: Explorer Scouts are the senior section of the Scouting movement, so an Explorer is a kind of Scout.
annotation.definitionFit: An explorer scouts out unknown territory, and Explorer Scouts are a section of Scouting.

entries.clue: Compete against women’s opinion (4)

indicatorNotes.against: one piece is placed up against the next

blocks.note: to vie is to compete
W = women, as on a toilet door

annotation.surface: A man argues against what women think.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Against' looks like opposition to women's opinion, but it only means VIE is set beside W.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the way you look at a question is your opinion on it.

entries.clue: Swap skilled occupation (5)

blocks.note: a verb: to exchange one thing for another
a noun: a craft such as plumbing or carpentry

annotation.surface: Someone thinks about switching careers into a craft.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, changing jobs, but the verb and the noun are two separate meanings of TRADE.
annotation.definitionFit: To trade is to swap, and a trade is a skilled job like carpentry.

entries.clue: Age range for retirement? Exit is arranged before start of summer (7)

indicatorNotes.arranged: the letters of EXIT IS are arranged in a new order
indicatorNotes.start of: take only the first letter of summer

blocks.note: EXIT IS rearranged
first letter of summer

annotation.surface: Planning a departure from work at the start of summer, at the usual retiring age.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'age range' is loose: people usually retire somewhere in their sixties.
annotation.definitionFit: The sixties, ages sixty to sixty-nine, is the decade in which most people retire.

entries.clue: Grumpy about power increasing, curiously (12)

indicatorNotes.about: SURLY goes about, around, the other pieces

blocks.note: surly = grumpy; split around the rest
P = power, as in physics
rising = increasing

annotation.surface: Oddly, someone grows grouchier as they gain more power.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' in the surface, but it is the container instruction: the grumpy word wraps round the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: Curiously and surprisingly both mean in an unexpected way.

entries.clue: Clothes become old, stuff to throw away (7)

blocks.note: garb = clothes
to age is to become old

annotation.surface: Clothes that have grown old and worn out are fit only for the bin.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs straight on from wordplay to definition, so the whole line reads as one piece of advice about a wardrobe.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, more American than British: rubbish, household waste bound for the bin.

entries.clue: Let down by large debtor (5)

blocks.note: L = large, as on clothing sizes
a debtor is someone who owes, an ower

annotation.surface: Someone feels betrayed by a person who owes them a lot of money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Let down' reads as disappointed, but here it is the physical sense of letting a rope or bucket down.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the physical sense: letting something down on a rope, not disappointing someone.

entries.clue: Member of Tea Party’s implied threat? (3,6)

blocks.note: the surface hears the American political movement; the setter means the tea party in Alice in Wonderland
say the guest's title with a dropped H and it becomes a warning that the speaker is angry with some woman

annotation.surface: A political question about the menacing undertone of a Tea Party activist's words.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tea Party' suggests the American political movement, but it is the Mad Tea Party in Alice in Wonderland; the question mark flags the pun, MAD HATTER spoken as "mad at 'er", I'm angry with her.
annotation.definitionFit: The Mad Hatter is one of the guests at the Mad Tea Party in Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

entries.clue: Unqualified, having unchecked power (8)

blocks.note: without reservation or limit, as in an unqualified success
describes a ruler no parliament can restrain, like a despot

annotation.surface: A ruler with no qualifications holds total power.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unqualified' tempts as 'lacking qualifications', but here it means without reservation.
annotation.definitionFit: Absolute means total and unreserved, and an absolute ruler's power has no check on it.

entries.clue: One has a blade, decapitating wild pig (3)

indicatorNotes.decapitating: cutting off the head removes the first letter

blocks.note: BOAR without its first letter B

annotation.surface: A hunter with a blade beheads a wild boar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blade' suggests a knife or sword for the killing, but it is the flat end of an oar.
annotation.definitionFit: An oar has a blade, the flat part that pushes the water.

entries.clue: Gave general idea of unpopular policy decision to begin with (8)

indicatorNotes.to begin with: only the letter decision begins with is used

blocks.note: out = out of favour
a line is a policy, as in the party line
first letter of decision

annotation.surface: A minister sketches an unpopular policy decision before announcing it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is political throughout, which hides that 'unpopular' is just OUT.
annotation.definitionFit: An outline is a sketch of the main lines only, so giving one is giving the general idea.

entries.clue: To some extent ignore conjunction (3)

indicatorNotes.To some extent: only part of the next word is used

blocks.note: the letters sit in the middle of this word, after IG and before E

annotation.surface: An instruction to partly disregard a joining word.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer sits in the middle of one word, 'ignore'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this negative joining word is one of the coordinating conjunctions, with and, but and or.

entries.clue: Splits up unmatched clothing (9)

blocks.note: a verb: divides, parts company
a retail term: tops, skirts and trousers sold singly to mix and match, not as a suit

annotation.surface: Someone sorts a pile of odd clothes into groups.
annotation.walkthrough: Separates is a retail word for tops, skirts and trousers sold individually to mix and match, rather than as a set.
annotation.definitionFit: To separate is to split up, and separates are clothes not sold as a matching set.

entries.clue: Cut carefully round advertisement for row of shops (6)

indicatorNotes.round: 'round' means surrounding: the cutting word is placed round the advertisement

blocks.note: to pare is to trim carefully
ad = advertisement

annotation.surface: A sign-maker neatly trims a poster advertising a local shopping street.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a parade is a short row of shops, often under flats along a street.
annotation.definitionFit: A British sense: a shopping parade is a short row of shops along one side of a street.

entries.clue: Offered pound for hammer (5)

blocks.note: gave = offered
L = pound, from the Latin libra, as in £

annotation.surface: Someone bid a pound for a hammer, perhaps at a car-boot sale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pound' and 'hammer' both suggest hitting, but pound is the money, L.
annotation.definitionFit: A gavel is the small hammer an auctioneer or judge bangs.

entries.clue: Conceited and idle (4)

blocks.note: big-headed, full of self-regard
futile or empty, as in idle threats

annotation.surface: A description of someone both big-headed and lazy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Idle' suggests lazy, but here it means futile, as in an idle or vain boast.
annotation.definitionFit: Vain means conceited, and also futile, as in a vain hope.

entries.clue: Moving about USSR, Scotsman perhaps used this? (7)

annotation.definition: Moving about USSR, Scotsman perhaps used this?

indicatorNotes.Moving about: the letters of USSR move about into a new order

blocks.note: USSR rearranged
Ian is a typically Scottish name

annotation.surface: A Scot travelling around the Soviet Union wonders which language he'd need.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: a Scot moving about the USSR would have used the local language.
annotation.definitionFit: Russian was the main language of the USSR, so a visitor there would use it.

entries.clue: Sons have scattered (4)

blocks.note: S = son, as in family trees
to own is to have

annotation.surface: A family whose sons have moved away all over the place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scattered' reads as describing the sons, but it is the definition: seed is scattered when planted.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: seed is scattered over a field when it is planted by hand.

entries.clue: Doctor, highly talented but not good, failed to settle (7)

indicatorNotes.but not: 'but not' means excluding: the talented word appears except for its G for good

blocks.note: Dr = doctor
GIFTED without G (good)

annotation.surface: A gifted but flawed doctor never put down roots anywhere.
annotation.walkthrough: G for good is a standard abbreviation, so 'not good' takes the G out of GIFTED.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who drifted moved from place to place and failed to settle.

entries.clue: Turn round using wide part of foot (5)

blocks.note: W = wide, a cricket extra
the heel is part of the foot

annotation.surface: Someone spins round on a broad heel.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket a wide is a ball bowled out of the batter's reach, scored as W.
annotation.definitionFit: Troops or birds that wheel are turning round in an arc, pivoting on one end of the line.
